chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter III
paragraphs: The fundamental significance of the European events at the start of the nineteenth century lies in the mass movement of European peoples from west to east and then from east to west. The initial impulse for the westward movement came from France. For the French to unite into a military force capable of invading the East, they first needed to combine into a sufficiently large group, renounce their established customs and traditions, and—through the process of war and campaigning—develop a leader who could stand at the head of the coming military movement.

And beginning with the French Revolution, the old, inadequately large group was destroyed along with its old customs and traditions. Step by step, a larger group was formed with new customs and traditions, and a man was produced who would stand at the head of that group and of the coming westward-to-eastward movement.

A man without convictions, without habits, without traditions, without a name, and not even a Frenchman emerges—by what seem the strangest coincidences—from the turmoil of French political parties. Without joining any of them, he is carried forward to a prominent position.

His colleagues' incompetence, his opponents' weakness and insignificance, the brazenness of his lies, and his dazzling, self-confident narrow-mindedness raise him to the head of the army. The brilliant quality of the soldiers in the Italian campaign, his opponents' reluctance to fight, and his own childish boldness and self-assurance win him military glory. Countless so-called coincidences accompany him everywhere. The disfavor into which he falls with the rulers of France works in his favor. His attempts to change his career path fail: he isn't accepted into the Russian army, and his appointment to Turkey comes to nothing.

On his return from Italy he finds the government in Paris dissolving; everyone in it is being inevitably swept aside and destroyed. And by coincidence, an escape from this dangerous position presents itself in the form of a pointless, purposeless expedition to Africa. Again, the same so-called coincidences attend him. The impregnable island of Malta surrenders without a shot; his most reckless orders are crowned with success. The enemy fleet, which later won't let a single boat slip past, now lets an entire army through. In Africa, a series of crimes are committed against the practically defenseless inhabitants. And the men who commit these crimes, especially their leader, convince themselves that this is wonderful, that this is glory, that it resembles Caesar and Alexander the Great, and that it is fine.

This ideal of glory and greatness—which consists not merely in considering nothing you do to be wrong but in taking pride in every crime you commit, attributing to it an incomprehensible supernatural significance—this ideal, destined to guide this man and all who follow him, takes full shape in Africa. Whatever he does succeeds. The plague doesn't touch him. The cruelty of massacring prisoners isn't held against him. His childishly reckless, unprovoked, and ignoble departure from Africa—abandoning his comrades in misfortune—is counted in his favor, and again the enemy fleet twice lets him slip through. When, completely intoxicated by the crimes he has so successfully committed, he arrives in Paris with no plan at all, the dissolution of the Republican government, which could have swept him away a year earlier, has now gone so far that his mere presence there, standing outside any party, can only elevate him.
He had no plan; he was afraid of everything; but the parties seized upon him and demanded his participation.
He alone—with his ideal of glory and greatness forged in Italy and Egypt, his insane self-worship, his boldness in crime and frankness in lying—he alone could justify what had to be done.

He is needed for the role that awaits him, and so—almost against his will, despite his indecision, his lack of a plan, and all his mistakes—he is drawn into a conspiracy to seize power, and the conspiracy succeeds.

He is pushed into a session of the legislature. In a panic, he tries to flee, thinking himself finished. He pretends to faint and says senseless things that should have ruined him. But the once proud and shrewd rulers of France—feeling that their role is played out—are even more confused than he is, and fail to say the words they need to say to maintain their power and destroy him.

Chance—millions of chances—give him power, and all people, as if by common agreement, work to confirm that power. Chance shapes the characters of France's rulers, who submit to him; chance shapes the character of Russia's Paul I, who recognizes his authority; chance produces a plot against him that not only fails to harm him but strengthens his power. Chance throws the Duke of Enghien into his hands and accidentally compels him to kill him, thereby convincing the crowd more effectively than any other means that he has the right to rule, since he possesses the power and the will to use it. Chance arranges it so that though he strains every nerve to prepare an expedition against England—which would certainly have destroyed him—he never carries out that plan, and instead falls upon Mack and the Austrians, who surrender without a battle. Chance and genius give him victory after victory. Everything serves him. He is invincible.

Like probing movements before a battle, the western forces push eastward several times—in 1805, 1806, 1807, and 1809—gathering strength and growing. In 1811, the group of people formed in France fuses into one enormous mass with the peoples of central Europe. As this group grows, the man who stands at its head gains more and more justification for his power. During those ten years of preparation, this man forms connections with all the crowned heads of Europe. The rulers of the world, stripped naked by this man, try to oppose him with the ideals of reason and justice. But these seem weak and ridiculous before his ideal of glory and greatness, which makes no sense yet still exerts its force. In their efforts to show him that his plans are wrong, these rulers eagerly humiliate themselves before him. The King of Prussia sends his wife to seek the great man's mercy; the Emperor of Austria considers it a favor that this man accepts the daughter of the Kaisers into his bed. The Pope, guardian of all that the nations hold sacred, uses religion to promote the great man's power. It is not so much Napoleon who prepares himself for the fulfillment of his role as everyone around him who prepares him for the immense responsibility he is about to bear. There is no act, no crime or petty deception, that he commits which is not immediately reflected in the mouths of those around him as a great deed.

The invasion pushes east and reaches its ultimate goal—Moscow. The city is taken; the Russian army suffers heavier losses than the enemy had suffered in any previous war from Austerlitz to Wagram. But suddenly, instead of those strokes of chance and genius that had accompanied him so consistently through an unbroken series of successes toward his intended goal, an endless series of reverse chances occurs—from the cold he catches at Borodino to the sparks that set Moscow ablaze. And instead of genius, stupidity and cowardice appear, without parallel.
The invaders flee, turn back, flee again, and now all the chances work not for Napoleon but always against him.

A counter-movement then takes place from east to west, remarkably resembling the earlier movement from west to east. There are preliminary drives from east to west—similar to the probing movements of 1805, 1807, and 1809—before the great westward surge. There is the same fusion of smaller groups into an enormous one; the same rallying of the peoples of central Europe to the movement; the same hesitation midway; and the same increasing velocity as the goal is approached.

Paris, the final destination, is reached. Napoleon's government and army are destroyed. Napoleon himself no longer matters; all his actions are clearly pitiful and contemptible. But once again an inexplicable stroke of chance occurs. The allies detest Napoleon, in whom they see the cause of their suffering. Stripped of power and authority, exposed as a schemer and villain, he should have seemed to them what he had seemed ten years before and would seem a year later—an outlaw beyond the law. But by some strange coincidence, no one sees this. His role is not yet over. The man who ten years earlier, and one year later, was considered a brigand beyond the law is sent to an island two days' sail from France, which is given to him as his personal domain, with guards and millions that are paid to him for some unknown reason.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter IV
paragraphs: The flood of nations begins to subside into its normal channels. The waves of the great movement settle, and on the calm surface eddies form in which the diplomats float, imagining that it was they who caused the flood to recede.

But the smooth sea suddenly becomes turbulent again. The diplomats think their disagreements are causing this new surge; they expect war between their sovereigns; the situation seems unsolvable. But the wave they feel rising is not coming from where they expect. It rises again from the same source—from Paris. The last backwash of the movement from the west occurs: a backwash that will resolve the apparently insoluble diplomatic difficulties and put an end to the military movement of that era.

The man who had devastated France returns to France alone, without any conspiracy and without soldiers. Any guard could arrest him, but by some strange chance no one does, and everyone rapturously greets the man they had cursed the day before and would curse again within a month.
This man is still needed to justify the final collective act.
That act is performed.
The last role is played. The actor is told to take off his costume and wash off his makeup: he won't be needed anymore.

And some years pass during which this man plays a pitiful comedy alone on his island, scheming and lying to justify his actions when justification is no longer needed, and showing the whole world what it was that people had mistaken for strength when an unseen hand was guiding him.
The stage manager, having brought the drama to its close and stripped the actor, shows him to us.
"See what you believed in! This is he! Do you see now that it was not he but I who moved you?"
But dazed by the force of the movement, it was a long time before people understood this.
Still greater coherence and inevitability can be seen in the life of Alexander I, the man who stood at the head of the counter-movement from east to west.
What qualities were needed in the man who was to stand at the head of that movement from east to west, overshadowing all others?

What was needed was a sense of justice and sympathy with European affairs—but a broad sympathy, not dulled by petty interests; a moral superiority over the other sovereigns of the day; a mild and attractive personality; and a personal grievance against Napoleon. And all of this was present in Alexander I; all of it had been prepared by countless so-called coincidences throughout his earlier life: his upbringing, his liberal beginnings, the advisors who surrounded him, Austerlitz, Tilsit, and Erfurt.

During the national war he was inactive because he was not needed. But as soon as the necessity for a general European war arose, he appeared in his place at the right moment and—uniting the nations of Europe—led them to the goal.
The goal is reached. After the final war of 1815, Alexander possesses all possible power. How does he use it?

Alexander I—the peacemaker of Europe, the man who from his youth had striven only for his people's welfare, the originator of liberal reforms in his own country—now that he seemed to possess the power and therefore the ability to bring about the welfare of his people, while Napoleon in exile was making plans that would infallibly have made nations happy had he been able to carry them out—Alexander, having fulfilled his mission and feeling the hand of God upon him, suddenly recognizes the insignificance of that apparent power, turns away from it, hands it over to despicable men, and says only:
"Not unto us, not unto us, but unto Thy name!... I too am just a man like the rest of you. Let me live like a man and think of my soul and of God."

Just as the sun and each atom of light is a sphere complete in itself, yet at the same time only a part of a whole too vast for man to comprehend, so each individual carries within himself his own aims while serving a larger purpose that lies beyond human understanding.

A bee landing on a flower stings a child. And the child is afraid of bees and declares that bees exist to sting people. A poet admires the bee drinking nectar from the flower and says bees exist to gather the fragrance of flowers. A beekeeper, noticing that the bee collects pollen and brings it to the hive, says that the bee's purpose is to gather honey. Another beekeeper, who has studied the life of the swarm more closely, says the bee gathers pollen to feed the young and rear a queen—that its purpose is the continuation of the species. A botanist notices that the pollen-dusted bee fertilizes the pistil of a flower, and he sees this as the bee's purpose. Another, observing the migration of plants, sees that the bee helps in this process, and he may say that this is the bee's purpose. But the ultimate purpose of the bee is not limited to any single one of these things that human reason can discover. The higher the human intellect rises in the discovery of such purposes, the more obvious it becomes that the ultimate purpose is beyond our reach.
All that is accessible to us is the relationship between the life of the bee and other forms of life. And so it is with the purpose of historical figures and nations.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter V
paragraphs: Natasha's marriage to Bezukhov, which took place in 1813, was the last happy event in the old Rostov family. Count Ilya Rostov died that same year, and—as always happens—with the father's death, the family fell apart.

The events of the previous year—the burning of Moscow and the flight from it, Prince Andrew's death, Natasha's despair, Petya's death, and the old countess's grief—fell blow after blow on the old count's head. He seemed unable to understand their meaning, and bowed his old head as if expecting and inviting more blows to finish him off. He appeared now frightened and bewildered, now unnaturally animated and energetic.

Natasha's wedding kept him busy for a while. He ordered dinners and suppers and obviously tried to appear cheerful, but his cheerfulness was no longer infectious as it had once been; on the contrary, it made those who knew and loved him feel sorry for him.

When Pierre and his wife had gone, the count grew very quiet and began complaining of depression. A few days later he fell ill and took to his bed. From the start, despite the doctor's reassurances, he knew he would never get up again. The countess spent two weeks in an armchair by his bed without undressing. Every time she gave him his medicine he sobbed quietly and kissed her hand. On his last day, weeping, he begged forgiveness from his wife, and also—though his absent son was not there—from his son Nicholas, for having squandered the family's fortune, which was the main thing he felt guilty about. After receiving communion and last rites, he died quietly, and the next day a crowd of acquaintances came to pay their final respects to the deceased. All those acquaintances who had so often dined and danced in his house, and who had so often mocked him behind his back, now said with a uniform feeling of inner self-reproach and tenderness: "Well, say what you like, he was a wonderful man. You don't find people like that anymore... And who doesn't have faults?"
It was precisely when the count's financial affairs had become so tangled that no one could say what would happen if he lived another year that he unexpectedly died.

Nicholas was with the Russian army in Paris when the news of his father's death reached him. He immediately resigned his commission and, without waiting for it to be accepted, took leave of absence and went to Moscow. Within a month of the count's death, the full scale of the financial chaos became clear, astonishing everyone with the enormous total of petty debts whose existence no one had suspected. The debts were twice the value of the estate.

Friends and relatives advised Nicholas to renounce the inheritance. But he considered such a refusal an insult to his father's memory, which he held sacred, and so he would not hear of refusing. He accepted the inheritance along with the obligation to pay the debts.

The creditors, who had been silent so long—restrained by the vague but powerful influence the count's careless good nature had exerted on them while he lived—now all rushed to press their claims at once. As always happens in such cases, a rivalry sprang up over whose claims would be paid first, and the very people who—like Mitenka and others—held promissory notes they had received as gifts now proved to be the most aggressive creditors. Nicholas was given no peace and no quarter. Those who had pitied the old man—the cause of their losses, if losses there really were—now fell mercilessly on his obviously innocent young son, who had voluntarily taken on the debts.

None of Nicholas's plans succeeded. The estate was sold at auction for half its value, and half the debts still remained unpaid. Nicholas accepted thirty thousand rubles from his brother-in-law Bezukhov to pay off the debts he considered genuinely binding—real debts to real people. And to avoid going to prison for the remainder, which he couldn't pay, he entered the civil service.

Returning to the army, where he would have been made colonel at the next vacancy, was out of the question, because his mother now clung to him as her only hold on life. And so despite his reluctance to stay in Moscow among people who had known him before, despite his distaste for the civil service, he took a minor government post, removed his beloved hussar uniform, and moved with his mother and Sonya into a small apartment on the Sivtsev Vrazhek.

Natasha and Pierre were living in Petersburg at the time and had no clear idea of Nicholas's situation. Having borrowed money from his brother-in-law, Nicholas tried to hide his wretched circumstances from him. His position was all the more difficult because, on his twelve-hundred-ruble salary, he had to support not only himself, his mother, and Sonya but had to shield his mother from their poverty. The countess could not imagine living without the luxuries she had known since childhood. Without understanding the difficulty, she kept demanding a carriage she no longer had to send for a friend, expensive delicacies for herself, and wine for her son.

Sonya kept house, waited on her aunt, read to her, endured her moods and secret resentment, and helped Nicholas hide their poverty from the old countess. Nicholas felt irredeemably indebted to Sonya for everything she was doing for his mother, and he admired her patience and devotion. But he tried to keep his distance from her.

He seemed in his heart to blame her for being too perfect, because there was nothing to blame her for. She had all the qualities people are valued for, but little that could have made him love her. He felt that the more he appreciated her, the less he loved her. He had taken her at her word when she wrote giving him his freedom, and now treated her as though everything between them had been long forgotten and could never, under any circumstances, be repeated.

Nicholas's financial situation kept getting worse and worse. The idea of saving something from his salary turned out to be a fantasy. Not only did he save nothing, but he even ran up small debts to meet his mother's demands. He could see no way out of his situation. The idea of marrying a rich woman, which his female relatives suggested, disgusted him. The only other way out—his mother's death—never entered his mind. He wished for nothing, hoped for nothing, and deep down took a dark, grim pleasure in stoically enduring his position. He tried to avoid old acquaintances with their expressions of pity and their offensive offers of help, avoided all entertainment and amusement, and even at home did nothing but play patience with his mother, pace silently around the room, and smoke pipe after pipe. He seemed determined to maintain within himself that gloomy state of mind in which alone he felt capable of bearing his situation.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: At the start of winter, Princess Mary came to Moscow. From talk around town she learned of the Rostovs' situation and heard how "the son has sacrificed himself for his mother," as people were saying.

"I never expected anything less of him," Princess Mary told herself, feeling a joyful confirmation of her love for him. Remembering her close relations with the whole Rostov family, which had made her almost a member of it, she felt it her duty to visit them. But when she thought of her relations with Nicholas in Voronezh, she was afraid to do so. A few weeks after arriving in Moscow, however, she made a great effort and went to see the Rostovs.

Nicholas was the first to meet her, since the countess's room could only be reached through his. Instead of the pleased greeting she'd expected, his first glance showed a cold, stiff, proud expression she had never seen on his face before. He asked about her health, led her to his mother, and stayed for five minutes before leaving.

When the princess came out of the countess's room, Nicholas met her again and accompanied her to the front hall with marked formality and stiffness. He made no reply to her remarks about his mother's health. "What's that to you? Leave me in peace," his expression seemed to say.

"Why does she come prowling here? What does she want? I can't stand these ladies and all these social niceties!" he said aloud in Sonya's presence, clearly unable to suppress his irritation after the princess's carriage had driven away.
"Oh, Nicholas, how can you talk like that?" cried Sonya, barely hiding her delight. "She's so kind, and Mama is so fond of her!"
Nicholas didn't reply and tried to avoid any further mention of the princess. But after her visit, the old countess talked about her several times a day.
She praised her, insisted that her son must return the visit, and expressed a wish to see her often—yet always grew ill-humored whenever she actually started talking about her.
Nicholas tried to keep quiet when his mother mentioned the princess, but his silence irritated her.
"She's a very admirable and excellent young woman," said the countess, "and you must go and call on her. You'd at least be seeing someone, and I think it must be dull for you just seeing us."
"But I don't want to at all, Mama."
"You used to want to, and now you don't. Really, I don't understand you, my dear. One day you're bored, and the next you won't see anyone."
"But I never said I was bored."

"You just said yourself you don't even want to see her. She's a very admirable young woman and you always liked her, but now suddenly you've got some notion in your head. You hide everything from me."
"Not at all, Mama."

"If I were asking you to do something unpleasant—but I'm only asking you to return a visit. Simple politeness requires it... Well, I've asked you, and now I won't interfere anymore, since you have secrets from your mother."
"Fine, I'll go if you want me to."
"It doesn't matter to me. I only want it for your sake."
Nicholas sighed, bit his mustache, and laid out cards for a game of patience, trying to redirect his mother's attention to another topic.
The same conversation was repeated the next day, and the day after that, and the day after that.
After her visit to the Rostovs and the unexpectedly cold reception from Nicholas, Princess Mary told herself she had been right not to want to be the first to call.
"I expected nothing else," she told herself, summoning her pride. "I have nothing to do with him, and I only wanted to see the old lady, who was always kind to me and to whom I owe so much."

But she couldn't calm herself with these reflections. A feeling close to remorse troubled her when she thought of her visit. Though she firmly resolved never to call on the Rostovs again and to forget the whole matter, she felt herself constantly in an uncertain position. And when she asked herself what exactly was troubling her, she had to admit it was her relationship with Rostov. His cold, polite manner didn't come from his heart, she felt sure of that; it concealed something. She needed to find out what it was, and until she did, she felt she could not be at peace.

One day in midwinter, as she sat in the schoolroom supervising her nephew's lessons, she was told that Rostov had called. With a firm resolution not to betray herself or show her agitation, she sent for Mademoiselle Bourienne and went with her to the drawing room.
Her first glance at Nicholas's face told her he had come only to fulfill a social obligation, and she firmly resolved to maintain the same tone in which he addressed her.

They spoke about the countess's health, about mutual friends, about the latest war news. When the ten minutes required by propriety had elapsed—after which a visitor may rise—Nicholas stood up to say goodbye.

With Mademoiselle Bourienne's help, the princess had kept the conversation going quite well. But at the very last moment—just as he rose—she was so tired of talking about things that didn't interest her, and her mind was so full of the question why she alone was granted so little joy in life, that she suddenly fell into a reverie and sat there motionless, her shining eyes staring straight ahead, unaware that he had risen.

Nicholas glanced at her and, not wanting to seem to notice her distraction, said something to Mademoiselle Bourienne and then looked at the princess again. She still sat motionless, and a look of suffering showed on her gentle face. He suddenly felt sorry for her and had a vague sense that perhaps he was the cause of her sadness. He wanted to say something kind and comforting, but couldn't think of what to say.
"Goodbye, Princess!" he said.
She started, blushed, and sighed deeply.
"Oh, forgive me," she said, as if waking up. "You're going already, Count? Well then, goodbye! Oh—the cushion for the countess!"
"Wait a moment, I'll fetch it," said Mademoiselle Bourienne, and she left the room.
They both sat in silence, occasionally glancing at each other.

"Yes, Princess," Nicholas said at last with a sad smile, "it doesn't seem long ago since we first met at Bogucharovo, but how much has happened since then! We all seemed to be in such distress then—yet I'd give anything to bring back that time... but there's no bringing it back."
Princess Mary gazed intently into his eyes with her own luminous ones as he spoke. She seemed to be searching for the hidden meaning of his words—the meaning that would explain his feelings for her.
"Yes, yes," she said, "but you have no reason to regret the past, Count. As I understand your present life, you will always look back on it with pride, because the self-sacrifice that fills it now—"
"I can't accept your praise," he interrupted hastily. "On the contrary, I constantly reproach myself... But this isn't an interesting or cheerful topic."
His face resumed its former stiff, cold expression. But the princess had caught a glimpse of the man she had known and loved, and it was to him that she now spoke.

"I thought you would let me say this," she said. "I had grown so close to you... and to your whole family, that I thought you wouldn't consider my sympathy out of place. But I was mistaken," and suddenly her voice trembled. "I don't know why," she continued, recovering herself, "you used to be different, and—"
"There are a thousand reasons why," he said, placing heavy emphasis on the word "why." "Thank you, Princess," he added softly. "Sometimes it's hard."

"So that's why! That's why!" a voice whispered in Princess Mary's soul. "No, it wasn't only that warm, kind, open look, not only that handsome face that I loved in him. I saw his noble, resolute, self-sacrificing spirit too," she told herself. "Yes, he's poor now, and I'm rich... Yes, that's the only reason... Yes, if it weren't for that..." And remembering his former tenderness, and looking now at his kind, sorrowful face, she suddenly understood the reason for his coldness.
"But why, Count, why?" she almost cried, unconsciously moving closer to him. "Why? You must tell me!"
He was silent.

"I don't understand your 'why,' Count," she continued. "But it's hard for me... I have to be honest. For some reason you want to take away our old friendship. And that hurts me." There were tears in her eyes and her voice. "I've had so little happiness in my life that every loss is painful... Forgive me. Goodbye." And suddenly she began to cry and started toward the door.
"Princess, for God's sake!" he exclaimed, trying to stop her. "Princess!"
She turned around. For a few seconds they gazed silently into each other's eyes—and what had seemed impossible and remote suddenly became possible, inevitable, and very near.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter VII
paragraphs: In the winter of 1813, Nicholas married Princess Mary and moved to Bald Hills with his wife, his mother, and Sonya.

Within four years he had paid off all his remaining debts without selling any of his wife's property, and having received a small inheritance from a deceased cousin, he repaid his debt to Pierre as well.
In another three years, by 1820, he had managed his affairs so well that he was able to buy a small estate adjoining Bald Hills and was in negotiations to buy back Otradnoe—his lifelong dream.

Having started farming out of necessity, Nicholas soon grew so devoted to it that it became his favorite—and nearly his only—occupation. He was a plain, practical farmer. He didn't like innovations, especially the English methods that were then coming into vogue. He laughed at theoretical treatises on agriculture, had no interest in factories or expensive crops, and didn't obsess over any one part of his operation to the exclusion of the rest. What he always kept in mind was the estate as a whole, not any particular component. What mattered to him was not nitrogen in the soil or oxygen in the air, not special plows or fertilizers, but the principal instrument through which nitrogen, oxygen, plows, and fertilizers all worked—that is, the laboring peasant. When Nicholas first took up farming and began to understand its various branches, it was the peasant who especially engaged his attention. He saw the peasant not merely as a tool but as an end in himself and as a judge. At first he studied the peasant closely, trying to understand what he needed and what he considered good and bad, and only pretended to give orders while in fact learning from the peasants, their methods, and their language. Only when he understood the peasants' tastes and aspirations, had learned to speak their language and grasp the hidden meaning behind their words, and felt himself one of them, did he begin to manage them boldly—that is, to fulfill toward them the duty expected of him.

Guided by some intuitive gift, on taking over the estates he immediately appointed as bailiff, village elder, and delegate the very men the serfs would have chosen themselves if they'd had the right. And these appointments never changed. Before analyzing the chemical properties of manure, before exploring the principles of debit and credit (as he liked to mock), he calculated how many carts his peasants had and tried to increase their number; he kept the peasant families as large as possible and wouldn't allow them to split up; he was strict with the lazy, the vicious, and the weak, and tried to keep them out; and at sowing and harvest time he went out to the fields himself to oversee the work, studying the peasants' crops with the same attention he gave to his own.

He was as careful about the sowing and reaping of the peasants' hay and grain as his own, and few landowners had their crops sown and harvested as early, as well, or with as good a return as Nicholas.

He didn't like dealing with household serfs—the "drones," as he called them—and everyone said he spoiled them with his leniency. When a decision had to be made about a household serf, especially one who needed to be punished, he was always uncertain and consulted everyone in the house. But when it was possible to send a serf to serve as a soldier in place of a peasant, he did so without a moment's hesitation. He never felt the slightest uncertainty in his dealings with the peasants. He knew that every decision he made would be approved by all of them, with very rare exceptions.

He never let himself be harsh with someone or reward someone merely because he felt like it. He couldn't have said by what standard he measured what he should or shouldn't do, but the standard in his heart was firm and unwavering.
He would often speak with vexation about some failure or problem and say: "What can you do with our Russian peasants?" and imagine that he couldn't stand them.
Yet he loved "our Russian peasants" and their way of life with his whole soul, and for that very reason he had understood and adopted the one method of farming that produced good results.

Countess Mary was jealous of this passion of her husband's and regretted that she couldn't share it. But she couldn't grasp the joys and frustrations he drew from that world, so alien and remote to her. She couldn't understand why he was so particularly excited and happy when, having gotten up at dawn and spent the whole morning in the fields or on the threshing floor, he came back to tea from the sowing, mowing, or harvesting. She couldn't understand what made him so delighted when he talked enthusiastically about the prosperous, hardworking peasant Matvei Ermilov who had been up all night with his family carting sheaves, or about having gotten all his grain in before anyone else.

Still less could she understand why, despite his kind heart and readiness to anticipate her wishes, he nearly lost his mind when she brought him a petition from some peasant men or women who had come to her asking to be excused from work—why he, a kind man, stubbornly refused, telling her angrily not to meddle in what was none of her business. She felt that he had a world entirely his own, which he loved passionately and which was governed by laws she did not understand.

Sometimes, when she tried to understand him and spoke of the good he was doing for his serfs, he would get annoyed and reply: "Not in the least; it never entered my head, and I wouldn't lift a finger for their good! That's all poetry and old wives' nonsense—all that doing good for one's neighbor! I don't want our children to go begging; I want to build up our family fortune while I'm alive. That's all. And to do that, you need order, you need discipline... That's the point!" he would say, clenching his large fist. "And fairness too, of course!" he would add. "Because if a peasant is naked and hungry and has only one wretched horse, he's no good to himself or to anyone else."

And probably because Nicholas allowed himself no thought of doing good for others for virtue's sake, everything he did was fruitful. His wealth grew rapidly; serfs from neighboring estates came begging him to buy them. And long after his death, the peasants preserved a devoted memory of his management. "He was a real master... The peasants' affairs first, then his own. And he didn't let you get away with anything. A real master!"
